title: Missionaries of Saint John the Baptist v. Frederic
backgroundAndFacts:
The Missionaries of Saint John the Baptist, Inc. is a Catholic religious organization based in Kentucky. Joel Frederic and his wife (referred to as 'et ux.,' meaning 'and wife') brought a lawsuit against the organization after Frederic was dismissed from his employment or position with the group. The Frederics alleged state law tort claims arising from the termination. The central dispute concerns whether civil courts can examine and second-guess the reasons a religious organization gave for ending the employment relationship.

The case worked its way through Kentucky's court system, ultimately reaching the Kentucky Supreme Court, which issued a ruling on December 18, 2025 that was unfavorable to the Missionaries. The religious organization then petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court, arguing that the Kentucky Supreme Court's decision allowed civil courts to intrude into matters of internal religious governance and discipline—a result they say violates the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

The U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear the case, but limited its review to just the first question presented in the petition. The case has attracted enormous attention from religious liberty advocates across many faith traditions, with amicus briefs filed by evangelical Christian groups, Catholic organizations, Jewish groups, Muslim organizations, Sikh groups, and a coalition of twenty states—all expressing concern that the Kentucky decision threatens the ability of religious organizations to manage their own internal affairs without government interference.
legalQuestion: Whether a religious organization's internal employment decision—specifically the dismissal of an employee for reasons rooted in religious doctrine—is protected from state tort liability under the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause or the ecclesiastical abstention doctrine.
significance:
This case could significantly clarify—or expand—the constitutional protections that shield religious organizations from civil lawsuits when they make employment and disciplinary decisions rooted in their faith. Known broadly as the 'ecclesiastical abstention doctrine' or the 'ministerial exception,' these protections prevent secular courts from becoming entangled in disputes that would require judges to evaluate religious doctrine, church governance, or spiritual fitness. A ruling in favor of the Missionaries could strengthen these protections and make it harder for former employees of religious groups to sue in state court.

The breadth and diversity of the amicus support—spanning Catholic, Protestant, Jewish, Muslim, Sikh, and Hindu organizations, as well as twenty state governments—reflects how high the stakes are perceived to be across different religious communities. A ruling narrowing First Amendment protections for religious employers, on the other hand, could open the door to increased litigation against churches, synagogues, mosques, religious schools, and faith-based nonprofits, forcing them to justify personnel decisions in secular courts under state tort law standards.

parties.party: Missionaries of Saint John the Baptist, Inc.
parties.coreArgument: The Kentucky Supreme Court's decision improperly allowed state tort claims to proceed against a religious organization for an employment decision grounded in religious doctrine, in direct violation of the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause and the long-established ecclesiastical abstention doctrine. Civil courts lack authority to evaluate the internal governance and disciplinary choices of religious organizations. The decision must be reversed to protect the constitutional right of religious bodies to order their own affairs.
supportingPoints: The First Amendment's ecclesiastical abstention doctrine bars civil courts from adjudicating disputes that require interpreting or evaluating religious doctrine, authority, or discipline.

Permitting state tort liability for religiously motivated employment decisions forces religious organizations to defend their doctrinal choices before secular judges, creating an unconstitutional burden on free exercise.
The ministerial exception and related constitutional protections apply broadly to employment relationships within religious organizations, not just to ordained clergy.
Allowing this lawsuit to proceed would deter religious organizations from making faith-consistent personnel decisions and effectively subject internal church governance to state oversight.

parties.coreArgument: The First Amendment does not grant religious organizations blanket immunity from state tort law when they harm employees through conduct that can be evaluated without resolving theological questions. The Kentucky Supreme Court correctly permitted the Frederics' claims to proceed because doing so does not require civil courts to pass judgment on matters of religious doctrine. Neutral principles of law can resolve this dispute without entangling the courts in ecclesiastical affairs.
supportingPoints: Courts can and should apply neutral, generally applicable tort principles to employment disputes involving religious organizations when no doctrinal inquiry is required.
The First Amendment protections for religious organizations are not limitless and do not categorically immunize all harmful conduct simply because it occurs in a religious employment context.
The ecclesiastical abstention doctrine is narrow and applies only where resolution of the dispute would require a court to interpret or weigh religious doctrine.
Permitting state tort claims to proceed respects both the rule of law and the Frederics' right to a remedy for the harms they suffered.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Hosanna-Tabor Evangelical Lutheran Church and School v. EEOC
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: This is the landmark case establishing the 'ministerial exception,' which bars employment discrimination suits brought by employees who perform religious functions, and is central to the Missionaries' argument that the First Amendment protects their personnel decision.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Our Lady of Guadalupe School v. Morrissey-Berru
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: The Court expanded the ministerial exception beyond formally ordained clergy to include lay teachers who performed religious duties, strengthening the Missionaries' argument that their employee falls within constitutionally protected employment relationships.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Serbian Eastern Orthodox Diocese v. Milivojevich
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: This case established the foundational principle that civil courts may not review ecclesiastical decisions of religious organizations regarding matters of church governance, discipline, and internal organization.

This foundational 19th-century decision established the principle of judicial deference to religious organizations' resolution of their own internal disputes, forming the historical basis of the ecclesiastical abstention doctrine.

This case defined the general framework for free exercise claims, holding that neutral and generally applicable laws do not require religious exemptions, but is relevant to the question of when the Free Exercise Clause does protect religious organizations from state law.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: This case reinforces that government action that targets or substantially burdens religious practice is subject to strict constitutional scrutiny, supporting the Missionaries' argument that imposing tort liability for religious employment decisions is unconstitutional.
